subject: research/garment-comfortcost
professional: a textile/clothing engineer working on personal thermal management (thermal-comfort modelling to ISO 7730/ISO 9920 plus apparel costing); first checks: does the PMV core reproduce the ISO 7730 reference values, is the comfort-equivalent shift the established 'corrective power' metric and is that literature cited, where do the treatment premiums come from, and does the cost chain (overhead, brand and retail multipliers) apply to an added fabric treatment the way apparel costing does

evidence.correctness: Ran `python3 experiments/run.py` (0.5 s); results.txt is rewritten identically (git status clean). Independent recomputation in scratchpad/gc_check.py (stdlib only): my own ISO 7730:2005 Annex D style PMV (iterative tcl, written from the standard's procedure, not from garment-thermal) gives -0.75 and +0.76 for ISO Table D.1 rows 1 and 2 (standard -0.75, +0.77, recalled from the standard), and with a bisection comfort-equivalent shift it reproduces the four insulation-only benefits exactly: warm 28 C thin +0.89, thick -1.24; cool 16 C thin -3.10, thick +4.04. Cost arithmetic by hand from garment-teardown's TRENCH numbers (2.9 m2 pieces / 0.80 marker x 1.03 waste = 3.7337 m2; overhead 0.25; 2.2 x 2.2): IR treatment added retail 271.07 designer / 44.80 replica (results +271 / +45); IR ceilings 1.05 / 6.35 USD/m2 (README 1.0 / 6.3); thin saving -253.0 at exponent 1, -142.6 at 0.5 (README -253, -143); replica white+thick 22.78 (README $23). Every number I recomputed matches. The optical levers (IR transmittance, emissivity, solar absorptance) were not recomputed independently: they rest on garment-thermal's unvalidated optical extension, whose signs I checked for physical sense only.
evidence.completeness: Everything the README lists runs: 7 tests pass (1.07 s); run.py reproduces results.txt byte for byte; figure.py run in a scratch copy reproduces costperdeg.svg (cmp identical); the five levers, three scenarios, joint (non-additive) benefit, cost model, premium ceilings, budget search and thickness-exponent sweep all exist and match the README text. Next steps (sourced premiums, gated lever, climate weighting) are listed as not done. The live page https://marisstella.app/research/garment-comfortcost/ could not be loaded (curl returned no connection through the proxy).
evidence.verification: `cd research/garment-comfortcost && python3 -m pytest -q tests`: 7 passed in 1.07 s. Six mutants with platform/ci/quality_mutate.py: caught 3 (sign of the benefit, inverted thickness price ratio, budget-search tie rule); survived 3: dropping the 25% overhead from added_fob, dropping the 2.2 retail multiplier from added_retail, and changing the low-emissivity lever from eps 0.2 to 0.5. No test pins any reported number (cost, ceiling or benefit) or checks run.py output against results.txt, so the cost chain that every dollar figure depends on is guarded only by sign and linearity tests.
evidence.craft: Read src/garment_comfortcost/cost.py (95 lines), tests/test_cost.py, experiments/run.py, experiments/figure.py, and the two upstream models. Small, readable, typed dataclass, exhaustive search is correct for 2^5 subsets. Defects: added_fob returns an unused `base` FOB and recomputes cost_breakdown on every call (cost.py:57,69); run.py section C re-derives the per-m2 retail cost inline instead of calling CostModel (run.py:60-61), a second copy of the cost formula; added_fob's thin/thick handling depends on lever order (last one wins) and is safe only because the search excludes the pair; run.py silences all warnings (run.py:12).
evidence.claims: Backed by files: every result number in the README (results.txt, recomputed above), '7 tests', 'seconds', the figure provenance, the non-additivity figures, the thickness-exponent caveat, the limitations (stylised premiums, inherited PMV caveats, shell-only costing, sunny scenario outside the index's range), and the AI-assistance disclosure. References carry DOIs and say 'not read in full'. Not backed or loose: (1) 'about six times harder ... because the retail chain scales the treatment's cost' (README.md:33): the ratio is 6.05 = 2.2 x 2.2 x 1.25, a quarter of it from the replica's zero overhead, not the retail chain; (2) 'the ranking among treatments is fixed by physics ... A treatment that works against the scenario's direction has no benefit at any price' (README.md:31): true for single levers, but results.txt section D shows infrared-transparent (alone -0.31 C in the sun) adding +0.33 C on top of white+thick (4.10 vs 3.77 C); (3) 'Cool room, replica: low-emissivity plus thin ... up to $20' (README.md:35) while results.txt shows nothing fits at $5 and $10. All low; the headline caveats are candid.
evidence.fitness: Job: a researcher wants to know whether a fabric lever is worth its price. The project's cost outputs are a linear rescaling of round-number premiums it invents (12, 6, 0.5 USD/m2); cost per degree = premium x 3.73 m2 x chain / benefit, so the only premium-free output is the break-even premium ceiling (section C), which is a one-line formula over garment-thermal's benefits. The comfort benefits themselves are garment-thermal's. Nearest prior work: the 'corrective power' of personal comfort systems (Zhang, Arens and Pasut 2015, Building and Environment, review of corrective power in non-neutral environments; cited from memory), which is exactly this comfort-equivalent shift in degrees and has a measured literature; techno-economic and setpoint-widening framings of thermal textiles (Peng and Cui 2020, Joule, 'Advanced textiles for personal thermal management and energy'; cited from memory). Neither is cited. Nothing here is new and sound enough to build on beyond the code join; it is a costing exercise far below the PhD bar in research/CLAUDE.md, and it ignores that file's 'run the numbers; don't stylise them' default for premiums that are findable (coating and functional-finish surcharges, nanoPE film prices), though section E does sweep x0.1 to x10.
evidence.domain: The PMV core matches ISO 7730 (recomputed). Departures a PTM engineer would flag: the comfort-equivalent shift is the established corrective-power metric but is not tied to that literature or to measured CP values; the sunny scenario (32 C, 1.6 met) is outside ISO 7730's validity range (stated); 0.5 clo is the whole ensemble's insulation but only the shell cloth is priced, and the shell price is scaled with ensemble clo (cost.py:66); treatment premiums are uncited round numbers and the apparel cost chain (overhead plus 2.2 x 2.2 keystone) is applied to a fabric surcharge without a source for that practice, which garment-teardown itself found does not reproduce reported prices. The method is internally consistent and honestly labelled, a practitioner would not use its dollar figures.

defects.what: The cost chain is untested: removing the 25% overhead or the 2.2 retail multiplier from the cost model leaves all 7 tests green, as does changing the low-emissivity lever value; no test pins a reported dollar figure or checks run.py output against results.txt.

Every dollar result rests on uncited round-number premiums (12, 6, 0.5 USD/m2) although research/CLAUDE.md asks for sourced parameters where findable; the comfort-equivalent shift is the established 'corrective power' metric of personal comfort systems (Zhang, Arens and Pasut 2015) and techno-economic PTM work exists (Peng and Cui 2020), neither cited or compared; the only premium-free output is a one-line break-even formula, so the research contribution is thin.

'A treatment that works against the scenario's direction has no benefit at any price' / 'ranking fixed by physics' holds only for single levers: IR transparency (-0.31 C alone in the sun) adds +0.33 C on top of white+thick, and section D selects it at $80.
'about six times harder ... because the retail chain scales the treatment's cost': the 6.05 ratio is the 2.2 x 2.2 chain times the designer's 25% overhead (the replica has none).
Cool-room replica frontier says low-emissivity plus thin holds 'up to $20', but results.txt shows nothing fits at $5 and $10 (low-e+thin costs $12).

Shell cloth price is scaled with whole-ensemble clo (0.5 -> 0.3/0.9) although only the shell is priced; with the order-dependent thin/thick handling this makes the thickness levers' costs an artefact (README says so for the exponent, not for the ensemble/shell mismatch).
run.py section C re-derives the per-m2 retail cost inline instead of calling CostModel (a second copy of the cost formula); added_fob computes and returns an unused base FOB.

verdict: A small, honest, reproducible costing exercise: every number I recomputed matches (an independent ISO 7730 PMV reproduces the ISO table rows and all four insulation-only benefits; the dollar figures, premium ceilings and thinning savings recompute by hand from garment-teardown's inputs), run.py and the figure reproduce byte for byte, and the limitations are candid. It does not meet the bar: verification is 2 (3 of 6 mutants survive, including removing the overhead or the retail multiplier that every dollar figure depends on), and as research it is far below the PhD bar: the cost outputs are a linear rescaling of invented premiums, the comfort benefits are inherited from garment-thermal, and the comfort-equivalent shift is the established 'corrective power' metric whose literature is not cited. Three README sentences overstate slightly (the 'six times' attribution, 'no benefit at any price' for single levers only, and the cool-room frontier range).
